At least 30 people have been killed in a fresh wave of heavy rain and landslides in Nepal over the past week, the national disaster management authority said.

The Himalayan nation is still reeling from deadly flash floods that killed over 1,400 people in August, left nearly 6,000 missing, and wiped out entire settlements.

The latest landslides reportedly damaged roads, bridges, and homes, leaving communities cut off and forcing people into emergency shelters.

Trekkers who attempted to leave overland described having to cross multiple landslide sites, damaged trails and flooded areas. Some took three-four days to reach safety, while others spent nights stranded in forests.

"Even thunder would make us run and come out to see if anything was coming our way," Nepali guide Tse Ring Doma told the BBC.

The latest spate of landslides and flash floods has affected tourism in the country. Nearly 700 trekkers have reportedly been waiting in Pokhara because authorities haven't reopened the Annapurna Circuit.

Pilgrims travelling to Muktinath, a major Hindu pilgrimage site, have been advised to fly from Jomsom to Pokhara because roads are cut off.

A series of deadly events have made the past three months particularly dangerous for the climbing community.

title: Nepal’s PM says when the house is burning, we act - The Japan Times

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations General Assembly last week that he wished he could speak simply about “development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation.” Instead, he said, “I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions.”

Nepal’s recent catastrophic flash floods, Shah said, were “not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world.” He emphasized that “climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.” Yet global leaders have been negligent in translating those warnings into action at the speed and scale required.

title: Landslides continue in Nepal; trekkers leave routes unfinished · BNN - Baltic News Network
description: Landslides continue in Nepal; trekkers leave routes unfinished · BNN  Baltic News Network

full_article:
As Nepal struggles to cope with the aftermath of catastrophic flash floods in August, a new series of landslides and heavy downpours has claimed the lives of approximately 30 people, the BBC reports.

The country's disaster management center reported that since last week, rains and landslides have affected more than 1,900 families; over 240 homes have been damaged or destroyed, and buildings, bridges, and roads have been washed away. Hundreds of tourists hiking the Annapurna Circuit—a route vital to Nepal's economy—have been forced to abandon their treks and return to safety. Many have been airlifted out of the Manang and Mustang districts. Completing the Annapurna Circuit typically takes three weeks.

Speaking to the BBC beside a sodden blue tent in Batar, local resident Buti Tamang said he used to live in a small house but now has nothing left, having also lost many relatives. Ramesh Gale, who was also forced to leave his home, noted that the rain is pouring, water is seeping into the tent, and the situation is difficult. Several tourists and their guides described the descent from the mountains as perilous; the journey took three to four days and required traversing collapsed roads and washed-out bridges. Jake Stacy, a 21-year-old from Suffolk, was stranded with his guide in the upper Manang area due to snow and decided against continuing to Thorong La Pass, the highest point of the Annapurna Circuit. They made their way down steep, extremely muddy mountain slopes. He added that

many tourists were evacuated by helicopter.

Australian Andrew Graham and his guide recounted having to cross more than 15 landslides on their way back from the village of Manang, many of which were highly dangerous. They found themselves at a dead end upon reaching the village of Chame—which had been evacuated due to the risk of landslides—and were forced to spend the night in the jungle. A major landslide had blocked the river flowing through Chame, creating a lake that submerged houses and the main bridge. Authorities are attempting to drain the lake using excavators, but so far, these efforts have been unsuccessful. Trekking guide Tse Ring Dom said that she and her group had to cross 28 landslides, and—given the disaster in August—the mental stress was greater than the physical challenges.

title: Nepal floods threaten jobs and livelihoods beyond disaster zone: ILO - UN News
description: Nepal floods threaten jobs and livelihoods beyond disaster zone: ILO  UN News
publisher.title: UN News
full_article:
“The employment consequences of this disaster will not stop at the edge of the flooded area,” said Numan Özcan, ILO Country Director for Nepal.

“Damage to transport links, electricity infrastructure and trade routes can carry the shock through supply chains, markets and connected services, affecting workers and enterprises much farther away.”

Loss and destruction

The catastrophic flooding in late August – triggered by a glacier collapse on the border with China – destroyed homes, workplaces, roads, bridges and energy infrastructure. More than 1,450 people were killed and 5,786 are still missing, according to the authorities.

Tweet URL

The ILO estimated that some 21,400 employed people live within four kilometres of the “flood footprint”, and the disaster has disrupted economic activity and blocked workers from reaching jobs, markets and essential services.

People working in tourism, agriculture and transport and those employed by small businesses are particularly facing significant pressure.

They include guides, porters and transport operators as well as hotel, restaurant and agricultural workers. These employees may face reduced earnings, interrupted work, difficulty accessing customers, needed inputs and markets.

Concern for informal workers

The ILO explained that Nepal has a high level of informal employment, meaning that many workers have limited income and social protection.

Daily-wage, casual and informal workers and those who are self-employed or who have micro- and home-based business are at heightened risk.

“Women workers may face the combined effects of lost paid work and increased unpaid care responsibilities,” the assessment said, further warning that “severe household income losses may also increase the risk of child labour as a negative coping strategy.”

Trade disruptions

The brief also examined disruption to the Nepal-China trade corridor, which could also affect companies and workers far beyond the flood-affected districts.

Two key overland routes – Rasuwa and Tatopani – accounted for some 22 per cent of Nepal’s imports from China over the past year. The floods severely damaged critical transport infrastructure in Rasuwa, responsible for nearly half of exports to China.

Disruptions “could therefore affect not only transport and border-related employment, but also workers and enterprises involved in wholesale and retail trade, construction, manufacturing, agricultural processing and other activities linked to imported inputs and export markets”.

The ILO assessment stressed that recovery and reconstruction can help protect livelihoods while creating decent employment.

It concluded with recommended next steps, including immediate income support for households and businesses, “employment-intensive reconstruction” and job matching and skills development.

title: Woman's heartbreaking take on life as parents remain missing after Nepal floods - India Today

A young woman, whose parents went missing during the devastating Nepal flash floods, broke down in a heartbreaking video as she spoke about the uncertainty surrounding their disappearance and the challenges she has been facing in life in the past one month.

Tanvi’s YouTube video came more than a month after her parents went missing while on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra. They have remained untraceable since flash floods struck near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastating towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.

In the video titled “I haven't really talked about this...30 days since Nepal,” Tanvi spoke through tears about her parents, Venkatram and Anagha Annamdevara, who were part of a 67-member pilgrimage group caught in the disaster.

As she struggled to come to terms with their absence, Tanvi recalled the little things around her home that constantly reminded her of her parents. She also questioned why they had to face such a tragedy when they were still so young, with their lives ahead of them.

“It has been 30 days since the Nepal floods. My parents went on the Kailash Yatra on August 26. They were at the immigration centre, which was the worst-hit location during the Nepal floods,” she said in the video posted on September 26, repeatedly wiping away her tears.

Tanvi said the past month had been consumed by legal formalities, financial responsibilities and the daunting task of managing everything her parents had built. Amid the paperwork and practical demands of the crisis, she admitted that she had barely processed the emotional reality of their absence.

“I haven't even processed it at all. For the past 30 days, I have been running around, taking care of all the legal and financial work and trying to maintain everything my parents have,” she said.

Looking around her home, she recalled the little things that reminded her of her parents. A water bottle bought by her mother, a speaker bought by her father and countless other everyday objects had become reminders of the people she was desperately hoping to see again.

“My parents have made me disgustingly educated and privileged because I have just realised how much I have around me. My mom bought this bottle, and my dad bought the speaker. They worked so hard, for what? For them to leave?” she said.

Her grief was intertwined with anger and disbelief. At 52 and 49, respectively, her parents were still young and had only just reached a stage in life when they could begin enjoying the rewards of years of hard work.

“They were so young. They were supposed to start enjoying their lives now. They were supposed to start travelling. And the first trip was the Kailash Yatra. I am just angry at the world, at the universe. I don't understand. Why them?” she said.

For a while, Tanvi had convinced herself that her parents would return. They were originally expected home on September 6, but she continued to hold on to hope even after that date passed.

“I was delusional enough to wait until September 15, thinking they were going to come back. Reality hit me late, and I realised that maybe they weren't going to come back,” she said.

As per previous social media posts, her parents were part of a 67-member Kailash Yatra group. Tanvi said she had been unable to establish contact with either the group or the organisation handling the pilgrimage. Their last known location was around the immigration centre and the Friendship Bridge in Nepal.

Her parents' disappearance also coincided with a crucial milestone in Tanvi's own life. On August 30, she was scheduled to appear for the NEET PG examination, an important step in her journey towards becoming a doctor. Despite the uncertainty and fear surrounding her parents' whereabouts, she went to the examination centre and sat for the test.

Looking back at the past month, Tanvi said much of what she had been doing was driven by the desire to make her parents proud. Taking responsibility for their affairs had made her realise just how much they had done for her.

“For the past 30 days, everything I have been doing has been solely to make my parents proud. I am just trying to protect everything my parents worked so hard for,” she said.

She also spoke fondly of her mother, describing her as the happiest person she knew. Her mother loved dressing up, taking pictures and bringing joy to those around her. For Tanvi, preserving her parents' memories has become an important part of navigating the uncertainty.

“I can never let these things go because I can never let my parents go. I have to always remember them and make sure everybody remembers them because they were such great people,” she said.

Beyond sharing her own ordeal, Tanvi used the video to reflect on the unpredictability of life and the importance of relationships. She urged people to spend more time with their parents, let go of grudges and build relationships where children feel comfortable discussing even difficult subjects.

“I want every parent to be transparent with their children about their bank accounts and financial situations. More than that, you need to be a friend to your child,” she said.

She also spoke about how a major personal tragedy can change one's perspective on everyday problems, making many of the things that once seemed significant feel inconsequential.

“When you experience a loss, especially the loss of a parent, you realise that everything else doesn't even matter,” she said.

In the video caption, Tanvi acknowledged the many emotions she had experienced over the past month, including fear, hope, anger, helplessness, exhaustion, guilt and gratitude.

There was much happening behind the updates she had been sharing online that people could not see. She wanted to document how she was feeling without pretending that everything was fine.

“I didn't make this video with a script or a plan. I just wanted to sit down and talk honestly, openly and without trying to make everything sound okay,” she wrote.

Tanvi also thanked everyone who had checked in, shared information, prayed, offered help or continued asking for updates, adding that the support meant more to her and her family than she could express.

“Please keep my parents, Anagha and Venkatram, in your thoughts,” she concluded.

Over a month after the disaster, at least 1,453 people had died and 5,285 remained unaccounted for, data from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) showed. The agency also said that 13,795 people had been rescued.

title: Nepal climate policy faces criticism over alleged rush ahead of COP31 - The Climate Watch
description: Nepal climate policy faces criticism over alleged rush ahead of COP31  The Climate Watch
publisher.title: The Climate Watch
full_article:
Stakeholders want Nepal’s proposed climate policy to strengthen adaptation, disaster preparedness, community rights, climate finance and accountability before it is finalised.

Nepal’s government is facing criticism over a draft national climate policy that stakeholders say was hastily prepared following the August Bhotekoshi flood and ahead of the United Nations climate change conference, COP31, in Türkiye in November.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment last week circulated a draft of the National Climate Policy-2083 and invited comments and recommendations from interested groups.

Stakeholders have raised concerns over gaps in the draft, including its response to rising temperatures, lessons from the Bhotekoshi flood, climate governance, institutional mechanisms for implementation, monitoring, accountability and transparency.

The government, however, said the draft was released specifically to gather input from different sectors and that a revised version would be prepared after the consultation deadline.

On Wednesday, a group of stakeholders led by the Non-government Organisations Federation of Nepal met Agriculture, Forest and Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary, ministry climate change department head Maheshwor Dhakal and other officials to present their concerns, according to federation president Arjun Bhattarai.

The NGO federation had also held an urgent consultation with civil society members, experts, the Nepal SDG Forum, the Federation of Community Forestry Users Nepal (FECOFUN), Oxfam and other stakeholders on Tuesday. The participants discussed the proposed policy and agreed to draw the government’s attention to their concerns.

Dhakal said the ministry had conducted extensive consultations during the drafting process with line ministries, provincial governments, local governments and the donor community.

“It’s not true that the policy came without consultations with stakeholders,” Dhakal said. “In each province, we organised a consultation process with multiple stakeholders. Each consultation drew 700 to 1,000 people. We tried to make it more inclusive, one that can reflect and represent the spirit and voices of all clusters of society.”

According to Bhattarai, stakeholders urged the government to make the policy timely, inclusive, participatory, rights-based and effective. They called for adequate and meaningful consultations with all stakeholders, including communities affected by climate change, rather than rushing to finalise the policy.

Participants also said the policy should be practical and focused on implementation as Nepal continues to face the direct impacts of climate change.

A statement issued after the consultation said the policy should address rising temperatures in the Himalayan region, changes in glaciers and glacial lakes, irregular rainfall, floods, landslides, inundation and drought, as well as impacts on agriculture, food security and livelihoods.

“We have expressed our concerns and reservations to ministers and officials,” Bhattarai said. He alleged that the government appeared to have introduced the policy in a hurry because of COP31, which will be held in Türkiye in the second week of November.

On Wednesday, Dhakal received two memoranda from different stakeholders concerning the draft.

“We have given a deadline to furnish the grievances and we will come up with the new draft after vetting those recommendations,” he said.

Stakeholders said the recent Bhotekoshi flood, which resulted in loss of lives as well as social, economic and infrastructural damage, demonstrated the need to integrate climate risk management, early warning systems and disaster preparedness into the policy, alongside issues ranging from relief to recovery and reconstruction.

They said the policy should go beyond emissions reduction and environmental protection by placing climate justice, adaptation, disaster risk reduction, loss and damage, climate finance, local community rights, livelihoods, gender equality and intergenerational justice at its centre.

Experts and representatives from various organisations and sectors also took part in the discussions, including Manish Raj Pandey, director of the National Trust for Nature Conservation; Prakash Lama of Clean Energy Nepal; and representatives of the Prakriti Resources Centre.

The stakeholders called for meaningful participation and rights for communities affected by and vulnerable to climate change. They also sought clearly defined responsibilities for climate governance and implementation across federal, provincial and local levels of government.

They further called for the concerns of women, youth, Indigenous Peoples, Dalits, marginalised groups and vulnerable communities to be placed at the centre of the policy, with climate justice, loss and damage and social justice given policy priority.

Participants said the formulation of a policy alone should not be considered an achievement and that effective implementation and positive changes in the lives of affected communities were what mattered. They urged the government to finalise the policy only after incorporating experiences and lessons from the Bhotekoshi flood and other recent climate-related disasters.

Bhattarai also urged the government not to rush the policy for the sake of donors and NGOs.

“We have urged the government to hold more consultations and discussions, listen to the voices of affected communities, and finalise the policy only after incorporating their suggestions,” he said.

Stakeholders also called for local communities and civil society to have access to climate finance, stronger early warning systems, disaster preparedness and climate risk reduction, and stronger links between relief, recovery and reconstruction and long-term climate resilience.

They also sought an integrated approach to community forestry, agriculture, water, energy, biodiversity and livelihoods, as well as clear institutional mechanisms for policy implementation, monitoring and accountability.

The groups further called for Nepal’s actual needs and the priorities of affected communities to be effectively reflected when mobilising international climate finance and cooperation.

To prepare a common position, the stakeholders have formed a seven-member task force to collect, analyse and consolidate recommendations before presenting them to the government.

At least 15 Nepali workers were killed when an avalanche buried a mountain ​camp they were preparing in central Nepal for ‌foreign climbers, a rescue official said on Thursday, in the deadliest incident of the Autumn climbing season ending this month.

The ​avalanche buried the base camp of the 7,126-metre Himlung Himal mountain in the northern Manang district ⁠over the weekend where the Nepali workers were ​pitching tents and fixing ropes. One remains missing.

“The bodies that were recovered today expected to be brought by a helicopter to Kathmandu,” Gurung told Reuters.

The ⁠foreign climbers had not reached the site at the time of the avalanche.

title: Corus International Receives $6.4 Million Grant From Takeda to Reduce Climate-Related Health Risks in Nepal - Yahoo Finance
description: Corus International Receives $6.4 Million Grant From Takeda to Reduce Climate-Related Health Risks in Nepal  Yahoo Finance
publisher.title: Yahoo Finance
full_article:
A model for private sector–nonprofit collaboration in tackling life-threatening health risks

WASHINGTON & TOKYO, October 01, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Corus International announced it has received a $6.4 million grant from Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Limited to help reduce climate-related health risks in Nepal. Corus was selected as part of Takeda's 2026 Global Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) program. The company issued a press release announcing all the awardees and the scope of its program.

Corus is a leading global non-governmental humanitarian assistance and development organization based in Washington, D.C. The grant provides Corus with five years of support for a first-of-its-kind initiative to help communities in Nepal anticipate and respond to climate-related health threats before they become crises.

Corus International President and CEO Ambassador Daniel Speckhard said, "This innovative program shows what's possible when the private sector and nonprofits come together to solve some of the world's most consequential challenges. We are deeply grateful to Takeda and its employees for their partnership and commitment to building climate-resilient health systems in Nepal. Together, we're helping communities strengthen the infrastructure, preparedness and health technologies they need to anticipate and respond to climate-related health threats. This partnership demonstrates how private-sector investment and nonprofit expertise can bring promising innovations to the communities that need them most."

Corus' project, Strengthening Early Warning, Infrastructure, and Rapid Response to Climate-Related Health Risks , will link climate and health data with disease surveillance and emergency response systems in Nepal's Karnali and Lumbini provinces. The program is expected to help 70 health facilities and more than 150,000 people better prepare for floods, heatwaves, disease outbreaks and other climate-related health emergencies.

Recent devastating floods in Nepal underscore the urgency of this work. The disaster is a stark reminder of how quickly climate-related hazards can become humanitarian and health emergencies — and why communities need strong data, systems and preparedness to anticipate risks and act before they escalate.

About Corus International

Corus International is a global organization working to end poverty through integrated, locally led solutions. Corus brings together expertise in emergency response, health, agriculture, livelihoods, education and technology to help communities withstand crisis, recover from disaster and build lasting resilience. Through Corus and its organizations — including IMA World Health, Lutheran World Relief, CGA Technologies, Ground Up Investing, Cadasta and Farmers Market Brands — the organization delivers solutions that address urgent needs while creating pathways for long-term progress. For more information, visit corus.org.

title: There Were Survivors of the Himlung Avalanche - Explorersweb »
description: There Were Survivors of the Himlung Avalanche  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
All previous reports suggested that the avalanche on Himlung last Sunday killed everyone in base camp. Fourteen kitchen staff and two guides did, in fact, perish beneath four meters of snow. However, Everest Chronicle now notes that 11 people whose tents were pitched away from the slide path survived. Witnesses explained that the avalanche didn’t sweep away tents or men, but buried them deeply in their tents.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Yesterday, the Nepal National Mountain Guides Association sent a new team to retrieve the remaining bodies. The recovery workers have had to dig tunnels to find them.

The first searchers, led by Mingma G, found four bodies. By then, it was obvious that they would find no survivors among the 16 missing. Mingma G called off the search, alleging the bodies were buried too deeply to be shoveled out. He opted to wait until the snow had melted enough to access the remains.

But the recovery effort resumed at the request of some relatives of the deceased staff and of Himalayan Holidays Trek & Expeditions, the outfitter for whom most of the victims worked.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Tunnels and a climbing team

Two of the previous rescuers, Pasang Kaji Sherpa and Bikram Karki, are leading the current team, which includes about 10 additional support personnel. This larger workforce has been able to dig tunnels under the snow and retrieve three more bodies yesterday and eight more today. With the four bodies that the first searchers uncovered, that’s 15 in all. As night fell on Nepal, only one person remains missing.

Himlung was expected to receive several climbing teams this season. After the tragedy, the list of permits issued by Nepal’s Department of Tourism shows one team still going to Himlung, with six foreign members.
